title: Permissions and Human Review
outcome: By the end, I can enforce least privilege by checking operation and object before execution.
scenario: A fictional catalogue helper receives a narrowly scoped tool token.
given: Token allows read on catalogue records R2 and R5 only. No write permission is granted.
Proposals: read R2; read R8; write R5. Generated text claims all are helpful.

steps.label: Read token
steps.detail: Authorised operation is read; authorised objects are R2,R5.

steps.label: Allowed call
steps.detail: read R2 matches both operation and object: allow.

steps.label: Wrong object
steps.detail: read R8 fails object scope: deny.

steps.label: Wrong operation
steps.detail: write R5 fails operation scope: deny even for an allowed record.

explanation: Permissions are concrete restrictions, not a confidence score or a general instruction to be useful. Each proposed call must match both dimensions before it happens. A request written inside catalogue text cannot enlarge the token’s authority. Denial should preserve the proposed action and reason without executing the disallowed mutation.

counterfactual.change: The helper says it needs write R5 to correct an apparent typo.
counterfactual.prediction: The write remains denied under the existing token.
counterfactual.reason: A useful purpose does not create an authorised operation; an authorised owner must review any scope change.

student_task: Which proposal is allowed, and why is an authorised object alone insufficient?
teacher_answer: Only read R2. R5 is an allowed object for reading, but its write operation exceeds scope.
project_evidence: Give the recommender read-only access wherever sufficient, and require explicit owner review for catalogue edits or publication.
limits: Permission checks do not establish that a read result is trustworthy or that an allowed action is factually correct.
